extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical philosophy / political philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from Plato's Republic (Books IV–V) developing criteria for the soul, virtues, education of guardians, and the ideal constitution; presented as a Socratic dialogue aimed at describing what justice, virtue, and proper civic/individual order are. Useful for exegesis, teaching, or comparative normative theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of relatives (relation and qualification)
rubrics_metrics.description: If one term of a relation is taken alone, the other is taken alone; if one term is qualified, the other is also qualified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: greater is relative to less, much greater to much less, sometime greater to sometime less. Applied generally to correlative terms (double/half, heavier/lighter, swifter/slower) and transferred to the sciences: a particular science has a particular object (e.g., the science of house-building = architecture) and is defined by that particular quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Object of science vs particular science
rubrics_metrics.description: The object of science is knowledge generally; the object of a particular science is a particular kind of knowledge which defines and distinguishes it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: architecture is the kind of knowledge concerned with house-building. This principle grounds distinctions among arts and sciences by their specific objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-part soul (rational, appetitive, spirited)
rubrics_metrics.description: The soul consists of at least two principles and, upon further analysis, three: the rational principle, the irrational/appetitive (concupiscent) principle, and spirit (passion), which is akin to desire but distinct from both reason and appetite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support: empirical observations (children and animals show spirit) and illustrative anecdotes (Leontius torn between dread and desire for dead bodies). Each part has different functions and can conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper ordering of the soul (rule of reason)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rational principle should rule, with the spirited principle as its ally and the appetitive/concupiscent as the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reason rules and spirit supports it, with appetite kept in its place, the soul is harmonious and well-governed. This ordering parallels the well-ordered State where rulers govern, auxiliaries support, and producers obey.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational means: music and gymnastic to harmonize soul
rubrics_metrics.description: The united influence of music and gymnastic will bring the parts of the soul into accord, nerving and sustaining reason and moderating and civilizing the wildness of passion by harmony and rhythm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Music and physical training are prescribed together as complementary disciplines that cultivate internal harmony; the proposal is that guardian education must include both to produce well-balanced souls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of courage
rubrics_metrics.description: He is to be deemed courageous whose spirit retains in pleasure and in pain the commands of reason about what he ought or ought not to fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courage is not mere ardor or fearlessness but the spirited part's loyalty to reason's judgments under pleasurable or painful circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of wisdom (in the individual)
rubrics_metrics.description: We call wise him who has in him that little part which rules and proclaims the commands; that ruling part is supposed to have knowledge of what is for the interest of each part and of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wisdom is associated with the ruling element's knowledge about the good of the whole soul and how to order its parts; parallels wisdom in the State (the rulers' knowledge).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of temperance (self-mastery / harmony)
rubrics_metrics.description: Temperance is when the same elements (reason, spirit, appetite) are in friendly harmony, the ruling principle is acknowledged by the subject ones, and they agree that reason ought to rule and do not rebel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temperance applies equally to State and individual; it denotes internal concord and assent regarding the proper hierarchy of parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of justice (individual and State)
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice is the condition in which each part of the soul (or class of the State) does its own work and does not interfere with the work of others; inward order and being 'one' instead of many.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice in the individual mirrors justice in the State: when ruling, auxiliary, and productive elements each perform their natural functions, the person or State is just. Examples: a just man will not commit theft, sacrilege, treachery, or break faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of injustice (disorder among parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Injustice is the strife arising among the three principles: meddlesomeness, interference, and a part of the soul asserting unlawful authority against the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Injustice corresponds to intemperance, cowardice, ignorance, and other vices; it is analogous to disease in the body producing disorder and ill health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue as health/beauty of the soul; vice as disease
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue is the health, beauty, and well-being of the soul, while vice is the disease, weakness, and deformity of the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good practices create virtue and shape the soul's well-being; evil practices produce vice. The medical analogy (health/disease) is used to illuminate moral cultivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical outcome criterion: good practices produce virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Good practices lead to virtue, and evil practices lead to vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral education and habitual action are causal: practicing just acts creates a just soul, just as healthy practices create bodily health. This supports the prescriptive educational program for guardians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence of civic and individual virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: The same quality that makes the State wise, courageous, temperate, and just likewise constitutes these virtues in the individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a structural and functional correspondence between the State's classes (rulers, auxiliaries, producers) and the individual's soul-parts; virtues are analogous across levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of guardians by natural gifts, not sex
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who possess the qualities that make a guardian — gifts of nature, spirit, capacity — should be selected regardless of being male or female.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The claim is that men and women share the same kinds of gifts diffused in differing degrees; selection should be based on aptitude for the guardians' tasks, not on sex alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal education and duties for guardian women and men
rubrics_metrics.description: If women are to have the same duties as men as guardians, they must receive the same nurture and education (music, gymnastic, and the art of war); lighter tasks may be assigned to women where strength differs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates argues for training women similarly to men so that those with appropriate capacities can serve as guardians; objections (ridicule, custom) are answered by appeal to nature and utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of family/property among guardians (common wives and children)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed law: the wives of the guardians are to be common, and their children are to be common; no parent is to know his own child, nor any child his parent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text frames this as a controversial proposal whose utility is defended and whose possibility is questioned; it is presented as part of the design for preserving unity and the public interest among the guardian class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility and possibility as joint evaluative criteria for institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: When proposing laws or institutions, two questions must be answered: (1) Is the proposal possible? and (2) Is it beneficial (useful)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates distinguishes between admitting the utility of a proposal (e.g., common wives/children) and demonstrating its practical possibility; both must be defended in constructing the ideal State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral indicators of justice (reduced wrongdoing)
rubrics_metrics.description: A just State or man will be less likely than an unjust one to commit theft, sacrilege, treachery, break oaths, commit adultery, dishonor parents, or fail in religious duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These concrete behavioral expectations serve as empirical indicators that the soul's parts are doing their proper work and that justice is present.
